strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem in generative modeling: adapting optimal transport ideas and likelihood/perplexity evaluation to discrete flow matching.

Theorem 3.1 establishes a clear formal link between the dynamic jump-cost minimization objective in discrete flows and the Kantorovich optimal transport formulation under coordinate-wise convex interpolants.

The derivation of the cross-entropy/perplexity upper bound (Theorem 4.1 and Eq. 24) adapts continuous-time Markov jump process variational bounds (Opper & Sanguinetti, 2007; Lou et al., 2024) cleanly to the discrete flow matching velocity framework.
The manuscript is well-written and mathematically straightforward to follow, with step-by-step proofs provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical evaluation: The paper does not include any experimental results, simulations, or empirical validations. While the submission proposes minibatch optimal transport coupling and a computable perplexity bound, neither is demonstrated on any synthetic or benchmark categorical dataset (e.g., text modeling benchmarks like Text8, LM1B, or protein sequence benchmarks).

Unverified practical utility of minibatch OT in discrete spaces: In continuous flow matching, minibatch OT straightens trajectories and enables fast sampling with few function evaluations. In the discrete setting, it is unverified whether the proposed minibatch OT coupling actually reduces sampling steps, accelerates inference, or improves sample quality, especially given the acknowledged issue of sparsity and low overlap in high-dimensional discrete token spaces.

Unassessed tightness of the perplexity bound: The paper derives an upper bound on cross-entropy/perplexity, but provides no numerical evaluation showing how tight or loose this bound is in practice compared to true log-likelihoods, variational bounds of discrete diffusion models, or autoregressive baselines.

Incomplete manuscript scope: Sections 3 ('Training Stability', 'Source Distributions') and 5 ('Future Work: Chains of Discrete Flows') outline algorithmic proposals and trade-offs in purely speculative prose without implementation, analysis, or algorithmic pseudo-code. The manuscript reads as an unfinished project proposal or initial theoretical note rather than a complete conference contribution.

strengths: Principled motivation: Addressing the non-deterministic nature of discrete flow paths and seeking to minimize transitions between dissimilar states is an important and timely direction for discrete generative modeling.

Formulation of token-similarity dynamic costs: Generalizing the dynamic jump penalty using arbitrary similarity metrics (such as embedding L2 distance and Hamming distance) provides an intuitive conceptual link between discrete flow dynamics and continuous optimal transport.

Theoretical derivation of the likelihood bound: Deriving a path-space KL divergence bound for discrete flow matching processes via continuous-time Markov jump processes (Theorem 4.1) adapts classical jump process theory to the discrete flow matching literature.
weaknesses: Complete lack of empirical validation: The manuscript contains no experimental results. Although the title, abstract, and introduction promise that the proposed minibatch OT strategy minimizes transitions and that the derived perplexity bound enables performance evaluation and comparison with other methods, no experiments (neither on toy synthetic problems nor on standard text datasets such as text8, LM1B, or WikiText) are provided to substantiate these claims.

Overstated theoretical connection to Benamou-Brenier: Describing Theorem 3.1 as a 'categorical-distribution version of the Benamou-Brenier theorem' is conceptually inaccurate. The Benamou-Brenier theorem is a variational duality establishing that the infimum of kinetic energy over all continuous fluid paths satisfying the continuity equation equals the Wasserstein-2 distance. In contrast, Theorem 3.1 simply computes the expected cost along a fixed, pre-specified convex interpolant flow (Gat et al., 2024); it does not establish a variational characterization over admissible velocities.

Unexamined bound tightness and computational feasibility: Path-space jump process KL bounds (such as Eq. 24) can often be loose or suffer from severe variance in high-dimensional discrete spaces. Without numerical experiments showing whether the bound is non-vacuous or useful as a proxy for test perplexity, the practical utility of Section 4 remains unverified.

Notational and mathematical inconsistencies: In Eq. (13), the cross-entropy loss is written with $\log p_{1|t}^i(x_0^i | x_t; \theta)$, which erroneously targets $x_0^i$ instead of $x_1^i$. In Eq. (21), the left-hand side is written as $-\log p_t(x_1; \theta)$ instead of $-\log p_1(x_1; \theta)$. There are also several typographical slips (e.g., 'moves form 0 to 1' on page 6, 'less ambitions' on page 7).

strengths: The paper targets important and timely challenges in discrete generative modeling: adapting optimal transport ideas to discrete flow matching and deriving tractable likelihood/perplexity bounds.
The manuscript is clearly structured, and detailed step-by-step mathematical proofs for Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Complete lack of empirical validation: The manuscript contains no experimental results whatsoever. Despite claiming to provide a framework for minibatch optimal transport in discrete flow matching and a computable perplexity upper bound to 'enable performance evaluation and comparison with other methods', the paper does not test these proposals on any toy, synthetic, or real-world datasets (e.g., text modeling benchmarks).

Limited theoretical depth of Theorem 3.1: The result does not establish a true Benamou–Brenier-style equivalence (which requires minimizing over all valid continuity equation velocity fields to yield the Kantorovich problem). Instead, it is a direct algebraic verification showing that evaluating the proposed dynamic penalty along the predetermined linear/mixture conditional path of Gat et al. (2024) integrates out to the expected static cost $\mathbb{E}[\sum_i s(x_0^i, x_1^i)]$.

Derivative nature of the perplexity bound (Theorem 4.1): The bound is a straightforward application of the standard path-space KL divergence for continuous-time Markov jump processes (Opper & Sanguinetti, 2007), which has already been extensively utilized in discrete continuous-time diffusion literature (e.g., Campbell et al., 2022; Lou et al., 2024).

Unsubstantiated speculative sections: Practical challenges mentioned in Section 3 (such as training stability under moving-average embeddings and choice of empirical/clustering-based source distributions) and Section 5 ('Chains of Discrete Flows') are discussed purely heuristically without formal algorithms, convergence guarantees, or experimental validation.

strengths: Principled and elegant theoretical formulation: The paper establishes a discrete analogue to the Benamou-Brenier theorem (Theorem 3.1) by minimizing dissimilarity-weighted jump transitions under convex interpolants, linking a dynamic path-length objective directly to static Kantorovich optimal transport.

Tackling a key open challenge in discrete flow matching (DFM): Because change-of-variables does not apply to discrete jump processes, likelihood evaluation in DFM has been intractable. The paper derives two computable upper bounds on cross-entropy/perplexity (Theorems 4.1, 4.2 and Propositions 4.3, 4.4), providing a grounded metric for model comparison.

Clever formulation of Multi-Mask Flows (DFM-MMLM): Standard masked flows have a degenerate Dirac source distribution that renders OT couplings trivial. Introducing disjoint multi-mask source tokens creates an entropy-rich source distribution that admits non-trivial OT pairings while strictly preserving time-independent predictive probabilities.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments are conducted on realistic text modeling setups (GPT-2 architecture trained for 400k steps on OpenWebText), evaluating both generative perplexity (using GPT-2 Large and LLaMA-3.1 8B as judges) and sample diversity (entropy). The scaling analysis of OT runtime overhead across batch sizes and sequence lengths is clear and practical.
weaknesses: Incremental gains of OT on Multi-Mask Flows: While minibatch OT yields substantial improvements for Bag-of-Words (BoW) source flows (reducing sampling steps up to 8x to match non-OT perplexity), the marginal improvement of DFM-MMLM-OT over standard DFM-MMLM is relatively subtle (e.g., in Table 3, GPT-2 judged perplexity improves from 143.48 to 141.92 at 1024 steps, and 155.45 to 153.51 at 128 steps).

Resource footprint of doubling vocabulary size in DFM-MMLM: Constructing $V_s = 50,257$ distinct mask tokens effectively doubles the vocabulary size to over 100k tokens. Although the paper notes that mask embeddings are untied from data embeddings, the added memory and computation overhead in the final logit projection layer deserves more explicit quantification and discussion.

Heuristic nature of bound evaluation for OT models: As acknowledged in Appendix C.3, computing the perplexity upper bound under minibatch OT is heuristic because minibatch OT defines an implicit coupling that cannot be exactly sampled at test time, introducing potential discrepancies when evaluating test sets.

strengths: Sound theoretical formulation bridging dynamic jump-rate minimization in discrete flow matching (DFM) with static Kantorovich optimal transport (Theorem 3.1) for arbitrary token-level similarity metrics, nicely generalizing the continuous Benamou-Brenier perspective to discrete state spaces with convex interpolants.

A creative and practical architectural solution (Multi-mask Flows, DFM-MMLM) that overcomes the inherent degeneracy of standard masked flows (where a Dirac source distribution precludes meaningful couplings), thereby unlocking the use of minibatch OT in masked discrete flow matching while preserving time-independent posterior predictions.

Rigorous derivation of computable upper bounds on perplexity and NLL for discrete flows (Theorems 4.1, 4.2 and Propositions 4.3, 4.4), generalizing discrete diffusion bounds to DFM and enabling direct, grounded likelihood-based comparisons with autoregressive baselines.

Thorough empirical validation, including proof-of-concept jump-count analyses on synthetic/character datasets, generative perplexity evaluations across step counts (8 to 1024), wall-clock computational scaling benchmarks, and ablation studies over OT batch sizes and solvers.
weaknesses: The 8-fold step reduction (1024 to 128 steps) is demonstrated primarily on Bag-of-Words (BoW) sourced flows, where initial trajectories are far more chaotic. For the stronger and more practical multi-mask models (DFM-MMLM vs DFM-MMLM-OT in Table 3), the performance improvement from OT is more moderate (e.g., generative perplexity improves from 155.45 to 153.51 at 128 steps and 143.48 to 141.92 at 1024 steps). Claims in the introduction and conclusion should consistently emphasize that the dramatic 8-fold step equivalence applies to BoW-sourced flows.

The multi-mask flow construction doubles the vocabulary size ($V = V_s + V_d = 50,257 \times 2 = 100,514$). While the paper addresses training time overhead, the exact implementation details regarding parameter count, memory footprint of the output classification head/logits, and whether logits over mask tokens are explicitly masked or discarded during training/inference should be more clearly documented in the main text.

Evaluations on OpenWebText are limited to context lengths of $L=128$ for generative quality (Table 3), with $L=1024$ primarily evaluated for baseline comparison in Table 2. Demonstrating generation performance at standard longer contexts (e.g., $L=512$ or $1024$) would strengthen the empirical impact.

strengths: Principled theoretical formulation: Theorem 3.1 establishes a Benamou-Brenier-type equivalence between the dynamic jump-rate minimization objective and the static Kantorovich optimal transport problem for discrete flows with convex interpolants, accommodating general token similarity functions (such as Hamming and embedding L2 distances).

Novel Multi-Mask Flow formulation: Standard masked discrete flow matching (DFM) has a Dirac source distribution, which collapses any non-trivial OT coupling. The proposed multi-mask flow (DFM-MMLM) elegantly restores non-trivial couplings while preserving the time-independence of predictive probabilities.

Tractable likelihood and perplexity bounds: The paper addresses a significant challenge in DFM (the inability to use instantaneous change-of-variables due to stochastic paths) by deriving two upper bounds on cross-entropy/perplexity, enabling principled intrinsic evaluation and cross-paradigm comparisons.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The experimental section is thorough, spanning synthetic/Morse proofs-of-concept to GPT-2 scale models trained on OpenWebText. It provides generative perplexities under multiple evaluator models (GPT-2 Large, LLaMA 3.1 8B), measures transport cost reduction, verifies sample diversity via entropy, and includes a detailed computational overhead analysis showing that minibatch OT adds minimal training time (~3.4%).
weaknesses: Incremental empirical gains of OT on masked models: While the step-reduction benefit of minibatch OT is substantial when using Bag-of-Words source distributions (achieving an 8-fold reduction in integration steps), the marginal performance gains of DFM-MMLM-OT over standard masked baselines (DFM-N, DFM-O, and DFM-MMLM without OT) in generative perplexity are relatively modest (e.g., Table 3 shows 141.92 vs. 143.48 at 1024 steps).

Coupling dynamics under learnable embeddings: As acknowledged in Section 7, when using learnable token embeddings for the cost metric, the distance geometry evolves simultaneously with model parameters. While minibatch OT remains stable empirically, the interaction between moving metric spaces and optimal couplings lacks formal convergence guarantees.

Overlap with concurrent bounds: The likelihood bound in Section 4.1 has conceptual and structural overlap with concurrent findings (e.g., Shaul et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2024; Haxholli et al., 2025), reducing to known diffusion bounds (such as MD4) in the absorbing/masked limit, which slightly tempers the standalone novelty of the bounding results.

Limited context length in core generation experiments: The main generation and OT scaling experiments on OpenWebText are conducted at sequence length L=128; evaluating full generation at standard language modeling sequence lengths (e.g., L=512 or L=1024) would better demonstrate scalability to longer sequences.
